OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Lachhman Singh, a former Member of this House on the 
21st February, 2006 at the age of 85 years. 
Born at Karanpur Village in the Panchkula District of Haryana, in January, 
1922, Shri Singh had his education at Mahendra College, Patiala. 
An agriculturist and a businessman, Shri Singh was an active social 
worker. He worked for the betterment of the deprived sections of the society, 
particularly, Harijans and Backward classes. Shri Singh was also associated with 
various social welfare and educational institutions. He was President of the 
Municipal Committee, Kalka, from 1957 to 1962 and Chairman of the 
Market Committee, Kalka, from 1962 to 1964. 
The legislative career of Shri Singh started with the membership of the 
Haryana Legislative Assembly. He was elected to that Assembly in the years 
1967,1977and 1982. He also had the distinction of serving as Minister in the 
State Government of Haryana and held various portfolios. He was the Minister 
of Transport and Public Relations in the year1967; Food and Supplies, 
Development and Panchayats, Labour and Employment, P.W.D., Building and 
Roads, Public Health, Fisheries and Dairy Development in the year 1977; and 
Industries and Public Health in the year 1982. 
Shri Singh served as the Deputy Chairman, Planning Board, Haryana from 
1995 to 1996 and also served as Chairman of the Committee on Public 
Accounts and the Committee of Priv ileges of the Haryana Legislative 
Assembly. 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
Shri Singh represented the State of Haryana in this House from April, 
1996 to April, 200? 
A widely travelled person, Shri Singh attended the World Assembly for Peace 
in East Berlin in the year 1969. 
In the passing away of Shri Lachhman Singh, the country has lost a noted 
social worker and an able administrator. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Lachhman Singh. 
I request Members of the House to rise in their places and observe silence 
as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Threat from Atmospheric Brown Cloud 
*342. DR. NARAYAN SINGH MANAKLAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Atmospheric Brown Cloud (ABC), a terminology 
generally used for the enormous blanket of pollution comprising ash, acids, etc., 
reduces the chances of monsoon rains substantially in the sub-continent thereby 
causing potential threat to the agricultural harvests; 
(b) if so, the measures taken/proposed to be taken by Government to tackle the 
threat; 
(c) whether any study to assess its impact on our country has been carried out; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
6 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (e) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Atmospheric Brown Cloud (ABC) refers to the high loading of 
pollutants in the atmosphere consisting of mixture of anthropogenic 
sulphates, nitrates, organics, black carbon, dust, fly ash particles, and 
natural aerosols such as sea salt and mineral dust. The brownish colour 
of cloud is due to the absorption and scattering of solar ultraviolet radiation 
by black carbon; soil derived dust, fly ash and nitrogen oxide. The ABC 
phenomenon occurs over several world regions, and is a seasonal 
phenomenon. 
The precise impacts of pollutant loading over monsoon rain and 
agriculture are still under study, and an international program has been 
initiated by the world community to better understand the origins, 
inventories and impacts of Atmospheric Brown Cloud. 
(b) The Government of India has taken several measures to reduce the 
pollutant loading e.g. introduction of tightened emission norms for vehicles, 
improvement in fuel quality in transport sector, use of cleaner fuels, 
introduction of electrostatic precipitators in thermal power plants, introduction 
of biogas plants and improved biomass stoves especially, in rural areas. These 
measures are aimed to improve the air quality by reducing the pollution 
loading. 
(c) to (e) A program named INDOEX  (Indian Ocean Experiment) 
undertaken during 1996—1999 with the participation by the Indian scientists, 
had drawn the attention of the international community on the issues pertaining 
to ABC. The preliminary investigati on of effects of pollution loading on 
winter rice and winter rains was undertaken for India through a modeling 
approach. 
India has also now formally joined the international effort through 
Atmospheric Brown Cloud (ABC) programme initiating more observations as 
well as undertaking impact studies. The programme covers both the 
observational as well as the impact studies on agriculture, hydrological cycle, 
health and monsoons/climate. However at this stage, it is premature to establish 
linkages between the Atmospheric Brown Cloud and climate change.

Leprosy patients in the country 
† *344. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 62 per cent of the world's leprosy patients are in 
our country; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the largest number of such patients are there 
in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal; 
(c) whether there is no qualitative change in its present status despite the 
leprosy eradication programme of Government; and 
(d) if so, the details of the existing number of Leprosy patients and their 
condition, State-wise and the details of action taken by Government in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) According to available data, as on 1st January 2005, India had 216445 
cases of Leprosy as against the global total of 286063 cases, thus contributing 
75% of the total cases globally. 
(b) The State of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and West 
Bengal currently have the largest number of leprosy cases in India. These States 
contribute to 42% of country's population and have 56% of total leprosy cases. 
However of the above States, the prevalence rate of leprosy in Madhya Pradesh 
was 0.87/10,000 population as on December, 2005, and, thus, the State has 
already achieved elimination of leprosy (i.e. prevalence of less than 1/10,000 
population). 
(c) and (d) No, Sir, There are substantive qualitiative changes in the 
strategy and content of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme. 
The National Leprosy Eradication Programme was previously a vertical 
programme where leprosy services were unavailable to large 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
segments of the population. In 2001-02, the programme was integrated with 
the General Health Care System throughout the country. After integration, 
leprosy diagnosis and treatment services are available through all Primary 
Health Centres and Government Hospitals throughout the country 
Earlier Dapsone was the only drug available for treatment of leprosy which 
had a very low cure rate. With the introduction of Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) in 
1982, a definite cure for leprosy was made available, Now leprosy patients can be 
successuflly treated by MDT within a duration of 6 months or 12 months 
depending on whether the case is multi bacillary or pauci bacillary. 
The Social stigma attached to leprosy was profound in previous years. 
Integration of leprosy services along with increased IEC efforts has helped to 
reduce the social stigma and has increased voluntary reporting resulting in timely 
treatment and reduction in disability rate. 
The National Leprosy Eradication Programme diagnoses and treats leprosy 
patients and releases them from treatment on completion of the therapy. As on 
31st December, 2005, the country has achieved elimination of leprosy at the 
national level with a prevalence of 0.95 cases/10,000 population. The State-
wise list of leprosy cases as on 31st January, 2006, is given in Statement-I.

(a) the names of the rail lines that are under conversion from metre gauge

Statement

Eastern Region have been taken up. 
(i) Lumding-Silchar-Jiribam and Badarpur-Baraigram-Kumarghat (409

(ii) Rangia-Murkongselek with linked fingers from Balipara to

(d) if so, the details thereof indicating the action plan of the Centre to help this backward

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Yes, it is a fact that Orissa Government proposes to formulate a project on reduction of child 
mortality with the assistance of World Bank to check the high infant and maternal mortality 
rate in the State. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Ms. Pramila Bohidar. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
The project proposal for reduction of child mortality is under formulation taking 
into account different components, such  as improvement in the quality of 
ante-natal and post-natal care, training of tradational birth Attendants, 
improvement of routine immunization, strengthening the rural Health 
Infrastructure, improvement and co-ordination between the Health Workers and 
Anganwadi Workers, provision of Drugs at Sub-centre level, strengthening the 
Management Information System relating to Health Sector, Improvement of 
Inter-sectoral Co-ordina tion for achieving the reduction in infant mortality 
rate. The formulation of the new programme is under progress. Specific details 
can be known only after the project has been finalized. 
Government of India have recently launched the National Rural Health 
Mission (NRHM) in order to improve the availability of and access to quality 
health care. The Mission seeks to pr ovide effective health care to rural 
population throughout the country with special focus on 18 States, which have 
weak public health indicators and/or weak infrastructure. Orissa is one among 
the 18 States. The Mission also aims at  achieving effective integration of 
health concerns with determinants of health like sanitation and hygiene, 
nutrition and safe drinking water through decentralized district plans. 
The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme which focuses on 
reduction of infant and mortality rates is being implemented as a component 
of NRHM. The interventions for reducing child and infant mortality include 
immunization against six vaccine preventable diseases, control of deaths due to 
diarrhoeal diseases, and due to Acute Respiratory Infections (ARIs), eradication 
of polio, prophylaxis against blindness due to Vitamin A deficiency and 
essential new born care. As a part of  the second phase of RCH programme, 
the Integrated Management for Newborn and Childhood Illnesses is being 
implemented in the districts in a phased manner. 
The interventions for improving maternal health are essential obstetric care, 
skilled attendance at delivery, promotion of institutional and safe delivery, 
emergency obstetric care, provision of referral services to pregnant women 
with complications of pregnancy and provision of assistance to Below Poverty 
Line (BPL) families for institutional deliveries through the Janani Suraksha 
Yojana. 
32 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Rs. 40.5 crores have been released to Orissa for implementation of the 
above mentioned activities in the year 2005-06. 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: Sir, the maternal mortality rate in Orissa is very 
High. It is 361 per one lakh live births in Orissa, while it is only 76 in Tamil 
Nadu and 29 in Gujarat. Orissa is a backward State and does not have the 
required resources to upgrade its medical facilities to control this high rate. In 
this context, I would like to ask the hon. Minister what is the action plan of the 
Centre to extend the required help to Orissa State to control the high maternal 
mortality rate in Orissa. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, it is precisely for this that we have 
launched the National Rural Health Mission to bring down the infant 
mortality rate and the maternal mortality rate, in fact, the total fertility rate of 
the pupulation. These are going to be the three focuses of the National Rural 
Health Mission which I have already mentioned in the earlier Sessions. Sir, 
this is one of the biggest programmes in the health sector. We are now taking 
this programme to the villages where there is no infrastructure. One of the 
priorities is to bring down the infant mortality rate. Now, we are trying to 
mobilise institutional delivery and incr easing the immunisation and, in fact, 
under the Janani Suraksha Programme we have said even the private sector could 
take up the delivery. Of course, today, the infant mortality rate is about 60 per 
thousand live births in the country. In Orissa, it is about 83 per thousand live 
births. Orissa has the highest IMR in the country. Sir, within the infant 
mortality rate, the neonatal mortality rate is quite high. In the country, the neo-
natal mortality rate is about 37 per thousand live births, that is, within the first 
28 days after the birth of the baby. Then, within that, fifty per cent of the 
neo-netal mortality rate is in the first three days. That is the most important 
period. That is why both the mother and child care is the main component of the 
reduction of the infant mortality. We are concentrating on this in our Rural 
Health Mission. That is one of the priorities that we have taken up. 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: What are the details of the Centrally-funded

New Pharmaceutical Policy 
*359. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether process for finalizing New Pharmaceutical Policy is on the anvil; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether there is any proposal to change the present methods of fixing 
prices of drugs; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) whether there is any proposal to allow the drug companies to fix the 
prices of drugs other than the Natio nal Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority 
(NPPA)? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (e) The process of formulating a New 
Pharmaceutical Policy has been set in motion. At present 74 bulk drugs and 
their formulations are under price control. These are called scheduled drugs and 
are specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Price Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95). Prices of these drugs are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPP A) in accordance with the provisions 
of the DPCO,95. The formula for calculation of retail price of formulations is 
given under para 7 of DPCO, 1995. 
Prices of non-scheduled bulk drugs and formulations are fixed by the 
manufacturers themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost 
54 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
of production, marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, 
market competition product innovation, product quality etc. The Government 
takes corrective measures where the public interest is found to be adversely 
affected. 
The Government constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint 
Secretary (Pharma) to examine the issu e of span of price control (including 
trade margin). Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. 
Pronab Sen, Principal Advisor, Planning Commission was also constituted to 
explore options other than price control to make available life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. 
Based on the recommendations of the Committee under the Chairmanship 
of Joint Secretary (Pharmaceuticals) and the Task Force under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal Advisor, Planning Commission 
and feedback from other stakeholders Government have formulated a draft 
National Pharmaceutical Policy, 2006 (PartA- excluding pricing) which has been 
circulated to various stakeholders seeking their comments. Based on the 
comments received the Government is likely to finalize the new Policy shortly 
including pricing mechanism to be adopted.

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Assistance to States for development of agriculture 
f2414. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the represen tatives of agricultural sector have 
put forward some demand before Government for development of this sector 
and making provision on this basis during discussion held prior to 
presentation of the Budget 2006-07; 
(b) if so, whether Government are aware of the said demands and whether 
Government are contemplating to provide economic assistance to States after 
considering new agriculture policy; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the progress made on the action taken/to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA):(a) to (d) In the two meetings held by the 
Ministry of Finance with the representatives of Agriculture/Agriculturists 
before the presentation of the Budget of 2006-07, the major suggestions which 
emerged relate to, credit at easier terms for farmers: coverage of risk related to 
farming; the need for easier access to high quality inputs by the farmers, 
including HYV seeds and access to irri gation; and encouragement for food 
processing. 
The Union Budget for 2006-07 has spelt out about Government's decision 
to ensure that the farmer receives shor t term credit at 7 per cent, with an 
upper limit of Rs. 3 lakh on the principal amount. For the current year, an 
amount equal to 2 percentage points of the borrower's interest liab ility on the 
principal amount up to Rs.1 lakh will be credited to the bank account of the 
farmer before 31st March, 2006. The Banks have been advised to do needful 
in this regard currently, National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) is

T2415. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SW ARAJ: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have not mentioned agriculture in their 
priorities in the economic survey; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether it will not have adverse effect on the development of 
agriculture? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) the importance of agriculture and 
allied sectors has been recognized in the Economic Survey 2005-06. The 
Economic Survey has stressed about the importance of enhancing agricultural 
growth in order to achieve the overall GDP growth rate in the range of 8 to 10 
per cent. The importance of horticulture in improving the productivity of land, 
generating employment, improving economic conditions of the farmers and 
entrepreneures, enhacning exports, and above all, providing nutritional 
security to the people has also been acknowledged. Referring to irrigation, 
which is one among the six components for development of rural infrastructure 
under 'Bharat Nirman' which aims at creation of 10 million hectare in the four 
years from 2005-06 to 2008-09, the target is expect to the achieved largely 
through completion of the on going major and medium irrigation projects. 
Citing the importance of marketing infrastructure, the Survey has pointed about 
the model law on agricultural marketing by the Ministry of Agriculture in 
consultation with State/UT Governments which is expected to enable 
establishment of private markets/ya rds, direct purchase centers, 
consumers/farmers markets for direct sale and promotion of public-private 
partnership (PPP) in the management and development of agricultural 
markets in the country. 
The Survey has also emphasized that the emerging areas in agriculture like 
horticulture, floriculture, organic farming, genetic engineering, food 
processing, branding and packaging and future trading have high potential of 
growth. Development of rural infrastructure, rural extension services and 
agro-based and food processing industries for harnessing this potential.

Efforts of Central Institute of Post Harvest Engineering and Technology 
(CIPHET) in developing technologies for minimizing losses in 
Agricultural Produces 
Central Institute of Post Harvest Engineering & Technology (CIPHET) was 
established on August 11, 1986 and started functioning w.e.f. December 29, 
1989 at PAU Campus, Ludhiana. Later ICAR decided to establish one more 
campus of CIPHET at Abhohar, which started functioning on March 19, 
1993. The Co-ordinating units of AlCRPs on PHT and APA are located at 
CIPHET, Ludhiana. The Institute has the following mandate. 
• To undertake basic, applied and adoptive engineering and 
technology research in postproduc tion sector of cereals pulses, 
oilseeds, fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops, 
products of forest origin, livestock and aquaculture products 
including agricultural structures and environmental control. 
• To act as National Institute for research, training and education in post 
harvest engineering and technolsgy. 
• To act as repository of information on post harvest engineering and 
technology. 
• to transfer technology and provide advisory and consultancy 
services. 
CIPHET has during the past 16 years carried out serveral R&D and HRD 
programmes to develop commodity and location specific technologies and 
demonstrate them to the stakeholders. A few of these technologies are listed 
below.

Agricultural Produces

• Development of pin mill for low temperature hygienic grinding of 
tough agricultural products.

2422. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will th e Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have conducted any survey to know the number 
of farmers living Below Poverty Line in Maharashtra; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the welfare schemes that have been implemented for the farmers of the 
State; and 
(d) the details of the financial assistance provided by the Central 
Government to the State during the last four years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) Plgnning Commission on the basis 
of the results of 'Situation Assessment Survey of Farmers', NSS 59th Round 
(Jan-Dec, 2003) has estimated the incidence of poverty among the farmers. 
According to the data available from that survey (Report No.495(59/33/4), it 
has been estimated that 22.84 percentage of farmers in Maharashtra live below 
the poverty line and the number of poor farmers is estimated approximately as 
77.12 lakhs. 
(c) This Ministry has been implementing schemes/programmes in 
Maharashtra State for increasing production of agriculture crops, which in turn 
benefit the farmers. Certain schemes which are being implemented

agriculture credit policy to provide timely and adequate credit support to 
farmers, various schemes under Horticulture Sector, Agriculture marketing and

Utilizing CWC godowns 
2423. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken steps to properly use Central 
Warehouse Corporation godowns in various places in Andhra Pradesh; 
(b) the steps being taken to review the contracts drawn up with private parties 
to only use their godowns for storing rice; 
(c) whether such un-profitable contracts will be reviewed; and 
(d) if not, the reasons for favouring such private parties? 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. The capac ity utilization of the 
Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) godowns is on an increase 
However, with a view to increase utilization of storage space belonging to the 
CWC, their following steps have been taken by the Government:— 
(i) CWC/Food Corporation of India (FCI) have been asked to de-hire private 
godowns (covered and CAP) where utilization is less than 25%. 
(ii) FCI has also been advised to give priority to hire CWC's godowns for 
storage of food grains. 
(b) to (d) FCI had entered into contracts with the Andhra Pradesh 
State Warehousing Corporation only and not with private parties to only 
use their godowns for storing of rice. Therefore, question of favouring 
the private parties and review of such contracts does not arise.

increase the production of foodgrains and in reducing the price of the 
foodgrains; and 
(d) the extent to which these have been helpful to the farmers and to put an 
end of suicides committed by them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) The State-wise number of ICAR Institute, 
State Agriculture University (SAU) and Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVKs) are

below). During 2005-2006, the total budget allocate of Indian Council 
of Agricultural Research (iCAR) Institutes was Rs.1,07,000.00 Lakhs 
including grant to Agricultural Universities and KVKs. 
102

(e) A number of high yielding improved crop varieties, crops production and 
protection technologies, cropping sequence and farm implements/ 
machineries for various agro-ecologies have been developed at ICAR 
Institutes and Agricultural Universities which are being demonstrated/ 
disseminated through KVKs and extension agencies. These lead to timely 
operations, higher input use efficiencies resulting into increased production and 
lower cost of production thereby higher financial gains to farmers. The 
production of foodgrains has increased from 171.04 million tonnes in 1989-90 
to 204.61 million tonnes in 2004-2005. As regards reduction in prices of 
foodgrains, the prices are determined by many important factors like cost of 
production, change in price of inputs, inter-crop price parity and demand and 
supply and international market price situations. 
(d) Technology of mixed farming including live-stock, horticulture and 
agro-forestry have helped the farmers to some extent in mitigating the effect 
of various biotic and abiotic stresses.

Non-payment of crop insurance claims 
2433. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR S ANGHI: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of crop insurance schemes in place for farmers; and 
(b) the details of complaints received from farmers in regard to non-
payment of crop insurance, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) National Agricultural Insurance Scheme 
(NAIS) is under implementation since Rabi 1999-2000 in the country. Main 
features of NAIS are annexed. Statement (See below). 
(b) All the admissible claims unde r NAIS are settled/paid as per 
provisions of the scheme. However, some complaints from farmers are 
received from time to time. Some of the complaints are given below:— 
• Farmers of Gujarat, Bihar, Karnataka, Rajasthan etc. have 
complained from time to time about delayed payment of claims. 
• Farmers in various States lik e Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Rajasthan etc. have complained regarding under payment of claims 
on account of incorrect submission of consolidated insurance 
proposals to the insurance company. 
• Farmers in some States want that loss assessment under the scheme 
should be made on individual basis. 
• Farmers in Gujarat, Maharashtra are not in favour of compulsory 
coverage of loanee farmers under the scheme. 
Statement 
Main Features of National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) 
• Scheme is available to all fa rmers—loanee and non-loanee both—
irrespective of their size of holding. 
• Compulsory for loanee farmers and optional for non-loanee 
farmers. 
• The Scheme is voluntary for the States/UTs. 
• Sum-insured may extend to the value of threshold yield of the area 
insured. 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
• Coverage of all food crops (cereals, millets & pulses), oilseeds and 
annual commercial/horticultural crops in respect of which past yield 
data is available for adequate number of years. 
• Among the annual commercial/horticultural crops, eleven crops 
namely cotton, sugarcane, potato, chillies, ginger, onion, turmeric, 
Jute, tapioca annual banana and pineapple are presently covered. 
• Basically all-risk insurance scheme covering all yield losses due to 
natural, non-preventable risks. 
• Premium rates are 3.5% for bajra and oilseeds, and 2.5% for other 
Kharif crops; 1.5% for wheat and 2% for other rabi crops. In case the 
rates worked out on the basis of actuarial data are less than the 
prescribed premium rate, the lower rate will be applicable.

f2441. SHRI MANGANI  LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of

state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in comparison to other States the foodgrains are 
lifted by Bihar in less quantity against that allocated and earmarked but only 25 
per cent of foodgrains actually reaches the real beneficiaries; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the beneficiaries in the State are not able to 
get full allocated foodgrains through Public Distribution System under various 
schemes of the Central Government; and 
(c) if so, the scheme-wise details thereof and the action Government 
propose to take in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) The Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) is operated under the joint responsibility of the 
Central Government and State Govemments/UTs. While it is the duty of the 
Central Government to provide foodgrains to the States/UTs, it is for the State 
Governments to lift the foodgrains and distribute the same to the targeted 
beneficiaries under TPDS. The offtake of foodgrains by the various State 
Government/UTs depends upon various factors like local availability of 
foodgrains, prices prevalent in the local market, food preferences of the people 
etc. The allocation of foodgrains to all States, including Bihar, is made by the 
Central Government under TPDS @ 35 kg per family, per month on the basis of 
poverty estimates of the Planning Commission during 1993-94 and population 
projection by the Registrar General of India as on 31.3.2000 or actual ration 
cards issued by each State/UT, whichever is less. The off-take of foodgrains 
by the State of Bihar during 2005-06 (Up to January 2006) under TPDS was 
22.21% [95.2% Antyodaya Ann Yojana (AAY), 30.4% for Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) and 0.85% for Above Poverty Line (APL)] against the national average of 
about 40% (85.09% for AAY, 74.6% for BPL and 16.9% for APL). 
(b) and (c) The offtake of foodgrains under AAY has been about 95% which 
is considered satisfactory. Besides AAY, the State Government has given 
priority to implementation of Annapurna Scheme under which t Original notice 
of the question was received in Hindi. 
140 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
the offtake during 2005-06 (upto January, 2006) is about 61 %. However, for 
BPL category under TPDS, the offtake has been 30.4% for which the State 
Government has been asked to take all possible measures to remove the 
bottlenecks and make TPDS a success in real terms 
A system to monitor distribution of foodgrains under TPDS is already in 
place. Planning and dispatch of the required number of rakes of foodgrains is 
made by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) every month for each consuming 
State/UT at an optimally feasible level, within the constraints of availably of 
rake's and other logistics in order to adequately cater to the requirements of each 
State/UT under the TPDS and other Welfare Schemes and with the aim of 
building up and maintaining the stocks level equivalent to three month's average 
requirement (Two months in respect of North-East Region). On receipt of any 
report regarding depletion of stock, the FCI is advised to prioritize the 
induction of rakes to such State/UT and whenever required, the Railway 
Board is also requested to take appropriate remedial action to augment the supply 
and induction of the rakes. 
The Central Government has also taken the following measures to ensure 
that the foodgrains reach the beneficiaries in the States/UTs:— 
(i) The Public Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001 was issued in 
order to streamline the functioning of the PDS and to make the 
same more effective and accountable. Any offence committed in 
violation of the provisions of the Order invokes criminal liability 
under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. 
(ii) The State Governments and the Union Territory Administration have 
been asked to actively involve the Panchayati Raj Institutions to 
monitor the functioning of the Fair Price Shops, as a measure of 
social audit. 
(iii) The State and Union Territories have also been asked to cons titute 
Vigilance Committees at the State, District, Block and FPS levels to 
oversee the functioning of PDS. 
(iv) With a view to efficiently  reaching PDS commodities to the 
consumers in a transparent manner, a model Citizen's Charter has 
been issued by the Central Government for adoption by the State 
Government/UT Administration. 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
(v) Under the Area Officers Scheme, the Senior Officers of the 
Government visits their allocated States/UTs to conduct review of the 
TPDS. The observations made by the Area Officers in their reports 
are sent to the concerned State Government/UT for taking necessary 
action. 
(vi) In the Regional Conferences he ld recently at Mumbai, Shimla, 
Thiruvanathapuram, Kolkata and Guwahati, the State 
Government/UTs were requested to take immediate necessary steps to 
curb diversion, through inspections, computerization and effective 
implementation of PDS (Control) Order.

Melting of ice of Poles 
2459. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that icelands of North and South Poles 
of earth are growing warmer these days; 
(b) if so, the extent to which the ice of these poles is expected to be melted 
during the coming five years; 
(c) the extent to which the levels of the oceans shall rise and most 
particularly the Indian Ocean, Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea; 
(d) the extent to which the coastal areas are expected to be adversely affected; 
and 
(e) what are Government's consideration in this regard for the protection of 
Indian soil? 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN M EENA): (a) and (b) The rising 
average global surface temperature also affects the North and South Poles of 
the earth. However, the studies based on various satellite data in Polar Regions 
have revealed that the two polar regions respond differently to increasing 
temperatures. While in Antarctica land ice is showing some melting signs in 
Western Antarctica Ice Sheet (WAIS) and Antarctic peninsular regions as 
compared to Eastern Antarctica. As far as sea ice is concerned, Weddell Sea is 
showing decreasing trend but Ross Sea is indicating increasing trend in sea ice 
extent. In Northern hemisphere, Arctic ice is melting at a faster rate leading to 
thinning of the Greenland Ice sheet and decrease in sea ice. 
(c) to (e) According to the third assessment report of the Inter 
Governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it is very likely that the 
20th Century warming has contributed significantly to the observed sea level 
rise, through thermal expansion of sea water and widespread loss of land ice. It 
has been observed that the global mean sea level had increased at an average 
annual rate of 1 to 2 mm during the 20th century. According to the Indo-UK 
study on climate change, mean sea level rise estimates (using past tide gauge 
data) were found to be slightly less than 1 mm per year in most of the stations 
analyzed along the Indian coast. 
Regional manifestations of the projections are not yet available with 
certainty and likewise the short term projections of five years. However, the 
preliminary studies carried out in the nature of vulnerablility assessment 
under the aegis of India's Initial National Communication project, it has been 
observed that the sea level rise (0.4-2.0mm/year) along the Gulf of Kutch and 
the Coast of West Bengal is the highest. On the other hand, along the Karnataka 
Coast, there is a relative decrease in the sea level. 
Future climate change in coastal zones is likely to adversely affect this region 
through erosion, flooding, submergence and deteriorating coastal ecosystems 
such as mangroves and salination. More comprehensive vulnerability 
assessments are expected to provide the basis for devising the adaptive 
strategies, beyond the current capacity for detailed modeling and vulnerability 
assessments. 
178

Preparation of photo identity cards of Tigers 
2461.  SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Wild life Institute of India has decided to prepare photo 
identity cards of all the Tigers of the country through new scientific 
techniques to have a more accurate count of the tigers living in the wild; 
(b) if so, whether the three techniques-computerized pugmark, camera traps 
and DNA tests have been tried elsewhere in the world; and 
(c) if so, what is the extent of accuracy about these methods? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) No, Sir. The new 
methodology of estimating tigers, co-predators, prey animals and evaluation 
of their habitat status has been evolved through collaborative research work 
between Project Tiger (Ministry of Environment and Forests) and the 
Wildlife Institute of India.This invo lves sampling and estimation of tiger 
density in different strata using a combination of 
180 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
methods, i.e. camera trap, digital photography of pugmarks to fix identities by a 
computer based recognition technique based on a mark-capture statistical 
framework, and correlation with other data, e.g. physical signs of tiger presence, 
prey-base, apart from DNA characterization of scats at places. The methodology 
has been approved by the Tiger Task Force constituted by National Board for 
Wildlife. 
(b) The three techniques viz., digital image of pugmark, camera traps and 
DNA scat analysis are scientifically valid methods for monitoring carnivore 
populations throughout the world. These have been used on mountain lion in 
the USA, jaguars in South America, tigers in India and South East Asia, and 
on wolves and bears in North America. 
(c) The new methodology would give 95% interval of statistical 
confidence of tiger population in the country.

Bird flu deaths 
2479. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of persons in the country who have so far been hit by bird 
flu, State-wise; 
(b) the number out of them who have scumbed to the disease, State-wise; 
and 
(c) the extent to which the Central Government have assisted the States, 
financially and by providing effective medicine for the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) There 
are no reports of any human cases of Avian Influenza (Bird flu) in the 
country. 
Death of poultry had been reported from Navapur Taluka of District 
Nandurbar, Maharashtra and Uchchhal Tehsil of Surat district in Gujarat. A 
series of strategic actions were initiated immediately on confirmation of Avian 
Influenza. The contingency plans were put into operation. Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, Government of India deputed its rapid Response Teams to 
Maharashtra and to Gujarat. The teams were in the field and assisted the State 
health Authorities in carrying out active surveillance to identify suspected 
cases among contacts of infected poultry. Adequate quan tity of Tamiflu and 
personal protective equipments were made available to both the States to meet 
the requirement. 
On 14th March, 2006 Department of Animal Husbandry notified outbreak 
of Avian influenza in Hated village (Chopada Taluka), Swada village (Raver 
Taluka) Salva village (Dharangaon Taluka) and Marul Village (Yaval Taluka) 
of Jalgaon District of Maharashtra. Animal Husbanry Department has initiated 
control and containment operations in 10 Kilometer radius of the four villages. 
Rapid Response Teams of Ministry of Health & F.W. and the State Government 
are in the field carrying out active house to house surveillance and 
Information, Education and Communication strategies. 
Required quantity of Tamiflu and personal protective equipments have been 
made available to the State Government. The situation is being closely 
monitored.

New health schemes for poor 
2480. SHRI E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any new health schems have been introduced for the benefit 
of the poorer sections of the society during the last four years particularly for

(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) In 
order to improve the existing healthcare delivery system and make health care 
accessible and affordable to the poorer and vulnerable sections of society 
particularly in the rural areas, a National Rural Health Mission was launched 
in April, 2005. This mission seeks to provide effective health care to rural 
population in all the States of the country including Tamil Nadu, with special 
focus on 18 States with poor health.indicators and weak health infrastructure. 
Under the strategy of NRHM, the gaps in the existing scenario of rural heath 
care is to be addressed through 2.5 lakh Accredited Social Health Activists 
(ASHA) to assist the Anganwadi Worker and ANM at village level to make the 
increased health services accessible to the rural people of the country, it is also 
proposed to upgrade CHCs to the level of India Public Health Standards 
(IPHS). NRHM has been launched for a period of 7 years (2005-2012) i.e. for 
two years of Tenth Plan and full Eleventh Plan. 
A World Bank assisted Integrated Disease Surveillance Project was 
launched in the year 2004-05 to strengthen capacity of all the States/UTs for 
Disease Surveillance. The project aims to strengthen public health laboratory 
services, train personnel and use information technology in surveillance. Early 
detection and timely response to outbreaks is expected to reduce spread of 
diseases in the Population including poorer sections of the society. 
Under the National AIDS Control Programme, the scheme to provide free 
ART to poor patients was initiated by the Government from April 2004. The 
scheme is being implemented in 52 health institutions of the country in 19 
States and a total of 23,784 patients are getting free ARVs.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per the 
report of HAO: Centre for Child Right, non profit society, 87 of every 100

of age. 
(b)As per the Sample Registration system of the Registrar General of India, 
the neo-natal mortality rate for the country has declined from 51 per thousand

(c) The Government has launched a new initiative, the integrated 
Management of Neo-natal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) in the country as part 
of the second phase of the Reproductive and Child Health Programme. 
IMNCI places specific attention to the ma nagement of newborn children in the 
community and promotes health care of newborns and children. 
In addition the ongoing programmes for maternal and child health care are 
being implemented. These are: 
1. Universal Immunization Programme (UIP). where immunization of 
children is carried out against six vaccine preventable diseases.

neonates (infants for the first 28 days of life). Training of district

Neonatology Forum. 
5. Prevention and treatment of micronutrient deficiencies, namely 
Vitamin A and iron. The activitie s undertaken are health and 
nutrition education, Vitamin A and iron supplementation, early 
detection and prompt treatment A and iron deficiency and 
treatment of infections.

introduction of complementary feeding thereafter are promoted as

UK medical journal, Lancet in its January 2006 issue has carried an article 'Low 
male to female sex ratio of children born in India: national survey of 1:1 million

natal sex determination followed by sex selective abortions of female fetuses, 
accounts for about 0.5 million missing female births yearly. The Government is 
aware of the problem and has been implementing the Pre-conception and Pre-
natal Diagnostic Techniques (PC & PNDT) Act 1994 in the country. 
(c) Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has undertaken training of

constituted as a mechanism to help A ppropriate Authorities in apprending 
actual wrong doer who are committing female foeticide/ abetting female 
foeticide.

this problem that has roots in social behavior and prejudices. A number of 
activities to create awareness on the issue are being undetaken. The

spread the message, requesting police training academies and schools to 
include the issues in curriculum of th eir training, telecas ting of video spots 
on private satellite channels and Doordarshan, and involvement of elected 
representatives etc. A 'Save the Girl Child' Campaign with a view to lessen

2504. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

identified five key genes that represent a breakthrough in treatment of TB;

and the progress made in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) It has been reported that 
Scientists at National Institute of Immunology have identified five genes that enable 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB causing bacterium of acquire the iron that it 
needs to sustain growth and promote infection. 
(b) Targeting genes within this cluster may represent a good strategy for 
eventual development of potential candidate drugs against tuberculosis and other 
mycobacterial infections. 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
(c) Mycobacteria have evolved sider ophores with lipid chain tails that 
enable them to exploit the macrophage's lipid-trafficking system to capture iron 
more efficiently. Now that these major siderophore genes have been defined as 
mentioned above, understanding the biosynthetic pathway that they are 
responsible for is the next step necessary in order to move eventually to the 
stage of developing small-molecule inhibitors with the potential to emerge as 
novel anti-tuberculosis drugs.

National Survey Report on 'The Extent, Pattern and Trends of Drug Abuse in India 
2004" sponsored by Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government 
and United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, demonstrates that alcohol, 
cannabis, opium, heroin are the major drugs of abuse in the country. The

borders, airports, foreign post offices, etc.

routes. 
(3) Improved coordination between the various drug law enforcement 
agencies in order to impart greater cohesion to interdiction. 
(4) Identification of illicit cultivation of the opium poppy and the wild 
growth of cannabis and eradication of these sources of supply.

analysis and dissemination of operational intelligence.

investigative assistance in ad ministering control over the 
movement of precursor chemicals.

233

(c) whether the existing legislati on The Cigarette and other tobacco 
Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade, Commerce, 
Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003' has been found ineffective to 
curb the sale of gutkha and pan masala in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The Central 
Government has received requests fro m Government of Maharashtra and 
Andhra Pradesh to ban manufacture and sale of gutkha and pan masala in the 
country. 
(b) The Central Committee for Food Standards which is a statutory 
body under the PFA Act, 1954, has recommended that Tobacco, Alcoholic 
beverages and Nicotine shall not be used as ingredients in the 
manufacture of proprietary foods (non-standardized foods). Gutkha is 
marketed as a proprietary food. 
Accordingly, draft rules further to amend PFA Rules, 1955 have been 
published in the Gazette of India vide notification GSR 694(E) dated 
28.11.2005 which inter alia propose that tobacco, alcoolic beverages and nicotine 
shall not be used as ingredients in proprietary food products. Proprietary food 
means a food which has not been standardized under PFA Rules 1955. The 
draft rules have been published for inviting objections/suggestions. 
(c) The Tobacco Control Act, 2003 does not provide for ban on 
manufacture, sale and export of gutkha and pan masala. However, it 
restricts the sale of tobacco produc ts including gutkha and pan masala, 
within 100 meters of education institutions. The State Governments are 
the implementing agencies of the provisions contained in the Act. 
Female foeticide in India 
2514. DR. VIJAY MALLYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the steps taken by Government to check the meanace of female 
foeticide in India; 
(b) whether it is a fact that British Asians are coming to India for sex 
determination and abortion of female foetuses; and 
234 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether Government have any plan to adopt British Laws and not allow 
parents to know the sex of the foetus? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The 
Government is implementing the Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic 
Tehniques (PC & PNDT) Act 1994 in the country which prohibits 
determination of the sex of the foetus. As per the provisions of the PC & PNDT 
Act, all units/clinics providing Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques services are 
required to be registered under the Act and those violating the provisions are 
punishable with a fine up to Rs. one lakh and imprisonment up to five years. 
As on 28.02.2006,28027 units/clinics have been registered and 383 court cases 
are filed for violation of various provisions of the Act. With a view to train and 
sensitize the lower judiciary about the PC & PNDT Act and the issue of female 
foeticide, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has undertaken training 
of trainers from State Judicial Academies. National Inspection of Monitoring 
Committee (NIMC) having representatives of Department of Women & 
Child Development, National Commission for Women, Indian Council for 
Medical Research, undertakes periodical visits to the districts with low child 
sex ratio to oversee the implementation of the Act at ground level and monitors 
the prosecutions launched against unregistered bodies and bodies violating 
provisions of the PC & PNDT Act/Rules. The National Support and 
Monitoring Cell is being constituted as a mechanism to help Appropriate 
Authorities in apprehending actual wrong doer who are committing female 
foeticide/abetting female foeticide. 
It is, however, recognized that mere legislation is not enough to deal with 
this problem that has roots in social behaviour and prejudices. A number of 
activities to create awareness on the issue are being undertaken. The initiative 
include meeting with the organizations working against sex selection, 
involvement of the medical professionals, religious leaders to spread the 
message, requesting police training academies and schools to include the issues 
in curriculum of their training, telecasting of video sports on private sate llite 
channels and Doordarshan, and involvement of elected representatives etc. A 
'Save the Girl Child' Campaign with a view to lessen son preference by 
highlighting achievements of young girls has been launched. District Magistrates 
have also been requested to regularly review the implementation of the 
PC&PNDT Act along with other programmes in their district. 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
(b) and (c) There have been reports about British Asians coming to India 
for sex determination and abortion of female foetuses. The Government is 
already implementing the Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(PC & PNDT) Act 1994 in the country which prohibits determination and 
communication of the sex of the foetus.

Jharkhand and Orissa. The raw material has to be moved by rail to eastern coastal 
sea ports and, then transported by sea route to New Mangalore Port. This is also 
uneconomical compared to sourcing of iron ore from Bellary Hospet region by 
rail. 
Movement of Iron Ore through Railway from Bellary Hospet region 
reduces pollution and road traffic congestion. For pollution control, KIOCL has 
put up water sprinklers at railway siding at Mangalore and the stockyards. It 
has also erected screens (HDPE Net) at railway siding for this purpose.

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION 
Panic over Bird Flu 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Members, I have to inform that Special 
Mentions will be taken up in the House today after the Listed Business 
before the House for the day is completed. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Sir, at the very outset, I would 
like to thank you for allowing me to make this mention. I think for the last 
one month or so this country has been witnessing a major noise on this 
whole question of bird flu in this country. Sir, it is perhaps not a coincidence 
that we had been hearing about all these major outbreaks of epidemics 
and so on in the Asian countries which are supposedly the emerging 
economies of the world today. First, Sir, we had heard about the SARAS 
and then the bird flu in a very big way. Now, Sir, if one goes by the actual 
figures of incidence of this kind of diseases and the extent to which the 
lethal nature of these diseases are being highlighted in the media, one finds 
that there is a mismatch between the actual incidence of the diseases 
286 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
and the extent to which the campaign is there and the information is 
being pandered in the media. Sir, I do not know, I mean, there seems to 
be an inseparable connection between the interests of some of the drug 
multinationals who seem to be behind this huge hullabaloo over certain 
diseases particularly that too in Asian countries and the extent to which 
they can profit and make super profit out of pushing the drug sales. Now, 
Sir, after we passed the third amendment here, we had a provision in the 
third amendment which was accepted by both House of the Parliament 
that for medical emergencies in countries like India and other developing 
countries we will have the provision of compulsory licensing for pandemics 
and epidemics breaking out and in the event of such public health 
emergencies we can actually give compulsory licence to drug companies 
so that cheap drugs could go for treating the people who will be afflicted 
by that epidemic. Now, Sir, there was an ongoing battle between one of 
the Indian drug companies, Cipla and the multi-national drug company, 
Roche over the patent of Tami flu which is supposed to be the only drug 
to be treating these bird flu cases. Sir, I have with me a campaign material 
from one Hetero drugs which has acquired the sub-licence from Roche, 
the German drug multinational company. They have in the material now 
come out with some Press reports. They have quoted in their own 
campaign material, The Times of India report dated 24th December 2005. 
They say that the company has already invested about 17 million dollars 
to produce the drug in India. Drug means Tami flu. When.launched, the 
drug could cost 12 US dollars per capsule. So, Hetero has invested 17 
million dollars after getting the sub-licensing from Roche and Roche was 
fighting an international case against Cipla for Tami flu drug. The company 
says,"We have committed to delivering one million capsules of Oseltamivir 
to the Government, which is the brand name for this drug, by 15th January 
2006. We will also start fulfilling or ders from LDCs, Least Developed 
Countries and developing countries from January". Now, 12 dollars per 
capsule is the price of this drug which Roche will be selling through their 
sub-licence, the Hetero drugs. They have also said — it is a report from 
the Financial Express — that the Swiss drug maker increase output, 
Governments around the world stockpile the medicine as the best defence 
against bird flu pandemic. They are saying that about one million such 
capsules will be acquired by India, by the middle of January and they are 
going to supply. I do not know that sudden outbreak of the bird flu or the 
reported outbreak of bird flu in this country in the end of January and its 
287 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
continuing campaign is really to gl oss over this aggressive marketing 
campaign of this multi national to really taking the gullible in this country. 
There has to be a thorough investigation as to what is the linkage between 
Government of India acquiring this one million capsules of Tami flu at the 
price of 12 million dollars and the so called outbreak of bird flu because 
95 samples of human incidence of bird flu were all found to be without 
any basis. So, Sir, I apprise the Gove rnment that this is the way the 
aggressive marketing campaign goes on and they have control over the 
global media and time and again this has happened. Therefore, Sir, it is 
a very urgent issue because 12 million dollars is not a small amount. I 
think, a thorough investigation has to be there to see what is the linkage 
between the report of these bird flu and possible incidence in human 
species and the purchase of this 12 million dollar worth of Tami flu by 
Roche who is in any case been contested by our own company, Cipla. 
They are prepared to sell Tami Flu at  120th of the price in the Indian 
market in the event of actual epidemic breaking out. I think, on this whole 
question the Government has to come out with some kind of a thorough 
investigation. So, I would like the Government of India to, actually, respond 
to this question. This is a very serious question. Thank you.

Discussion on working of the Ministry of Labour and Employment 
SHRI CHITTABRATA MAJUMDAR (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, just 
today the outcome Budget and the Performance Budget of the Ministry have 
been placed on the Table of the House. So, it is not possible to examine 
those Budget papers. However, what we have seen from our 
288 

[17 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
experience is that the functioning of the Ministry of Labour is not to protect 
the interests of labour. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIAN) in The Chair] 
But, whatever little things are done, it is only to protect the interests of 
the employers. Sir, the NCMP says and I quote, "The UPA Government 
is firmly committed to ensuring the welfare and well-being of all workers, 
particularly those in the unorganised sector who constitute 93 per cent of 
our workforce. Social security, health insurance and other schemes for 
such workers like weavers, handloom workers, fishermen and 
fisherwomen, toddy tappers, leather  workers, plantation labour, beedi 
workers, etc., will be expanded". 
Now, we find that in this year's Budget, the Hon. Finance Minister has 
provided only Rs. 1176.55 crores for labour welfare and Rs. 548.88 crores 
for social security and welfare. Out of Rs. 1176.55 crores for labour 
welfare, Rs. 840 crores is the cont ribution for the employees Pension 
Scheme for those who are covered under the EPF Act. The rest is 
accounted for industrial relations, working conditions and safety, labour 
welfare, labour education, etc. nothing is there for unorganised sector 
workers. 
Sir, Rs. 548.88 crores, meant for social security and welfare, includes 
Rs. 435.05 crores for pension and ot her benefits for freedom fighters. 
There is an allocation of Rs. 40.73 crores for children and women and 
Rs. 26.60 crores for the handicrafts. So, actually, for the unorganised 
sector workers, nothing is there in the Budget, though it has been promised 
that the Government will look and take steps for the betterment of the 
unorganised sector workers. 
Now, Sir, the NCMP further states on labour and I quote. "The UPA 
rejects the idea of automatic hire-and-fire. It recognizes that some changes 
in labour laws may be required but such changes must fully protect the 
interests of workers and families and must take place after full consultation 
with trade unions". 
Actually, what is its function? I do not understand whether the 
Government recognises the existence of trade unions or not. 
Yesterday, an incident happened in Ludhiana. The workers of Oswal 
woollen factory were agitating because some of their demands were not 
being met by the employers. The police lathicharged and arrested a large 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [17 March, 2006] 
number of workers, and even from the trade union office itself they arrested the 
workers. And various charges have been made against those workers. 
The case of Honda factory, which happened some time before, is well 
known to everbody. We find that with the indulgence of the State 
Governments, the authorities in the unorganised and the organised sector, even 
where multinationals are there, are not allowing the workers to form unions. 
Their unions are not getting registered by the Department. Even when the union 
is registered, the management does not sit with the unions to settle the disputes. 
When the disputes are raised with the Labour Commissioner, in many cases, 
the Labour Commissioner also does not take any initiative to convene a 
meeting and settle the dispute. But in many cases, when the meeting is 
convened, the management does not cooperate. And there are cases also, 
where with their intervention, some agreement was arrived at, even then, 
the management is not implementing those agreements. 
These types of incidents are happening everywhere around the country. Big 
multinationals are not allowing the workers to form their unions. And, what is the 
role of our Labour Department? We raised this issue, a number of times, with the 
Labour Department. But, the Labour department did nothing, actually. 
Sometimes, their reply is that it is the responsibility of the State Governments. 
We have All India Act, the Trade Union Act, the Industrial Disputes Act, but 
these Acts are not being implemented. If the States do not implement those, is 
there anything that can be done by the Labour Department at the Centre? 
We raised the issue that in Sikkim, the Trade Union Act is not being 
implemented, and the Industrial Disputes Act is not being implemented. 
Industries are there, workers are there, but they are not being allowed to form 
any trade union. So, disputes will be there, but where will those disputes be 
settled? We raised the issue with the Labour Department. But the matter has 
not been sorted out. The simple answer is that they have not introduced this

Need for early legislation on reservation for women in 
Parliament and State Legislatures 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR  (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, this is my last 
Special Mention as my tenure is going to end. I think, it deserves 
appreciation from the House. 
Sir, the subject of my Special mention is 'Need for early legislation on 
reservation for women in Parliament and State Legislatures'. The idea of 
making a legal provision for reservation of seats for women in Parliament 
and State Assemblies came into being when in 1993, one of the most 
important steps for the empowerment  of women and increasing their 
participation in decison-making was taken by reserving 33 per cent seats 
for women in Panchayati Raj and local bodies. Against all apprehensions, 
women succeeded in overcoming heavy odds to achieve good results in 
these intitutions. Later on, Shri H.D. Deve Gowda, in his tenure, as Prime 
Minister made a promise for reservation of seats for women in Parliament 
and the State Assemblies in 1996, and Shri l.K. Gujral gave the idea, the 
form of a Bill. The Bill, as wa s introduced in the past, envisaged 
reservations of 181 seats in the Parliament for women. Since then, there 
has been a lot of debate on the provisions of the Bill which lapsed on the 
dissolution of the last Lok Sabha. It is being said that some political parties 
are having reservations on the whole concept of reservation for women, 
but this cannot be the guiding fact for providing reservation to them. Do 
we always take decison when there is a consensus? 
Women constitute 50 per cent of our population. Reserving 33 per 
cent seats for them will be opening the doors of opportunity for political 
empowerment of half of the population. It will not only serve the cause of 
democracy as the Panchayati Raj institutions are doing at the gross root 
level, but will also go a long way in ensuing political equality through 
active participation of women from both urban and rural areas. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Government to bring forth the Women 
Reservation Bill in this session itself and pass it. 
Thank you very much, Sir.

Need for inclusion of Warangal and Tirupathi under Jawahar Lal 
Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR RE DDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, The Government of India has launched a 
programme for improving the standards  of cities and amenities to the 
people through the Jawahar Lal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission. 
It is very important to include cities like Warangal and Tirupathi of Andhra 
Pradesh in this programme. 
Tirupathi town of Andhra Pradesh is world famous for Lord 
Venkateswara Temple in Tirumala Hills, where around 50,000 people 
daily visit for darshan of the deity. The population of the town is around 
3 lakh. Similarly, Warangal town (Municipal Corporation) is a historic city 
and was the capital of the Kakatiya Dynasty of 10th Century and the city 
known for its Warangal Fort and Thousand-Pillar Temple. It is an important 
tourist town in Telangana area of t he State. The present population of 
Warangal is about 7 lakh. 
As Government of India has already constituted the National Steering 
Group (NSG), I once again request you to kindly consider inclusion of 
both cities of Tirupathi and Warangal of Andhra Pradesh in the category 
of 'C Selected Cities/UAs under the Jawahar Lal Nehru National Urban 
Renewal Mission. 
I request that the demand may be considered at the earliest. Thank 
you.

Need to retain exemption given to Cooperatives under the Income 
Tax Act 
SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, there are 31 State cooperative and 364 district cooperative 
banks in the country to support over one lakh primary agricultural 
cooperaties. Similarly, there are 1875 urban cooperative banks, out of 
which 1200 are so small that their deposits are less than Rs. 25 crores. 
Cooperative banks cater exclusively to small farmers, rural economy and 
people of limited income in the urban areas. They are local banks. Healthy 
cooperative banks ensure distribution of deposits that are mobilised locally 
to the economic activities in that place itself. This is very important since 
commercial banks, on the other hand, invariably help in resources that 
are mobilised in less developed areas to by used in richer and more 
prosperous areas. Absence of strong cooperative bank in local areas will 
only help this phenomenon. And, 40 per cent loans to small farmers are 
through cooperative banks. The rural cooperative banking system is still 
the mainstay of agriculture financing and rural economy, notwithstanding 
its perceived weaknesses. 
But, to the utter disappointment of cooperative banks, the finance 
Ministry is now proposing to tax profits of cooperative banks. This reported 
move would take away Rs. 500 crores from cooperative system, which 
otherwise help in improving the net worth of the cooperative banks and 
help in financing agriculture and other priority sector loans. The other 
point is, most of the cooperative banks, which will be forced to pay income 
tax, are only marginally healthy. If you impose income tax, they become 
even bankrupt. So, I request the Government of India not to amend 
Section 80(P) and maintain the status quo.

machinery in place for registration of marriages in every 
district in the country 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Prade sh): lakhs of girls in India 
believe that if boy and girl exchange 'Varmaala', or if boy puts Vermilion 
on the forehead of a girl, or if boy and girl perform 'Saat Phere' marriage

girls and girls are realising this often very late and, by that time, they

Supreme Court suggested to the Union and the State Governments for 
registration of all marriages, irrespective of personal laws and customs. 
This directive of the Supreme Court also helps in stopping child marriages. 
Registration of marriage should be the right of every girl. Making 
registration compulsory paves the way for marriage of only eligible 
couples. But, the question is how are you going to implement this important 
measure. The Government should implement this measure, irrespective 
of personal laws, by immediately setting up necessary machinery at district 
level, to begin with. I also suggest  that counselling centres should be

legislation should also be brought before Parliament. Poor and uneducated

established. I am just saying this because if the Centre leaves it to the 
States, they do not do it due to financial and other constraints. So, this 
has to be taken up by the Government of India on warfooting. Otherwise, 
this is also going to meet the same fate as the Child marriages Act.
